overview: The Ptolemies governed Egypt from Alexandria as Macedonian monarchs and Egyptian pharaohs. Their kingdom brought Greek-speaking rulers into a society with enduring Egyptian languages, temples and crafts. Surviving decrees and estate papers reveal both royal institutions and everyday work.

periods.title: The early royal dynasty
periods.summary: Ptolemy I took the royal title in 305 BCE. During the third century BCE, Alexandria grew as a royal center while the dynasty competed with other Hellenistic kingdoms.

periods.title: Later Ptolemaic rule
periods.summary: From around the start of the second century BCE, lost overseas possessions, rebellion and growing Roman influence changed the kingdom. Temple life and artistic production continued through these political pressures.

items.text: The Rosetta Stone preserves a priestly decree honoring Ptolemy V in 196 BCE. Soldiers found it reused in a fort at el-Rashid in 1799, so its discovery location is not the original setting of the decree.

Hieroglyphic Egyptian, Demotic Egyptian and Greek versions address different readers of the same royal decree. This is evidence of multilingual administration and priestly authority, not three different spoken languages.

Villagers digging for fertilizer uncovered the Zenon archive near ancient Philadelphia in 1914 to 1915. The documents illuminate a third-century BCE estate, but their exact original findspot was not recorded.

A lease copied in a lawsuit prepared by Zenon required tenants to grow wheat and barley and deliver grain rent at Philadelphia. Clauses about seed advances and outstanding debts reveal how agricultural work depended on both produce and credit.

The same document allowed recovery from debtors, their guarantors and their property. Read beside its crop instructions, it shows the unequal bargaining power behind estate production, rather than an idyllic picture of farming.
A papyrus dated 7 May 254 BCE records a stolen donkey. This small dispute survives because estate papers were kept, giving a glimpse of transport animals and ordinary losses outside royal histories.

Eratosthenes worked at the Alexandrian library in the third century BCE. He compared summer-solstice shadows at Syene and Alexandria with an estimated distance between them to calculate Earth's circumference.
His original measurement treatise is lost; the method survives in later authors. Uncertainty about the length of the stadium makes a single modern claim for his percentage accuracy misleading.
The sieve associated with Eratosthenes identifies prime numbers by removing multiples. It is a concrete example of mathematical reasoning connected with Alexandria's scholarly world.
Temple workshops made faience vessels and colorful glass inlays. Egyptian and Greek forms coexisted, and royal portraits could combine Greek hair with Egyptian poses.
Egyptian temples remained centers of scholarship and worship, supported by rulers who also promoted their own royal cults.

Zenon's files include letters about shipments of wheat and wine as well as official and personal business. Their survival connects agricultural production with transport and administration, rather than treating trade as an abstract royal achievement.

ending.text: Roman takeover in 30 BCE ended the dynasty after Cleopatra VII's defeat. Egyptian religious and artistic traditions continued beyond the change of rulers.
